def binomial_trailing_zeros(n, k, b):
    """
    Return the number of trailing zero digits of the binomial coefficient
    C(n, k) when it is written in base b (standard positional notation,
    no leading zeros).

    Equivalently: the largest integer t >= 0 such that b**t divides C(n, k).

    Input domain:
        n, k : integers with 0 <= k <= n <= 10**18
        b    : integer with 2 <= b <= 10**6

    C(n, k) itself can have hundreds of quadrillions of digits, so it must
    never be computed directly.  Note C(n, k) >= 1 always; the number 1 has
    zero trailing zeros in every base, so e.g. k == 0 or k == n gives 0.
    The base b need not be prime and may be a perfect prime power (e.g. 8
    or 9) or a mixed composite (e.g. 12): a trailing zero requires a full
    factor of b, so for b == 12 one factor 3 and two factors 2 are consumed
    per zero.

    The returned value is a single Python int.  There are no ties and no
    floating point anywhere.

    >>> binomial_trailing_zeros(9, 4, 6)
    1
    >>> binomial_trailing_zeros(10, 5, 10)
    0
    >>> binomial_trailing_zeros(1000000000000000000, 500000000000000000, 2)
    24
    """
